audience.programmeDescription: Economie en Bedrijfseconomie at Tilburg University combines economic theory, accounting, finance, business and data analysis. Students choose an Economics or Business Economics specialisation after the common first year. This comparison shows the Dutch-language Bedrijfseconomie route.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR options combine economics with business and data, public institutions and social policy, or practical finance and quantitative methods. Tilburg retains a more specialised accounting and business-economics sequence and a required 12-EC thesis. Shared rows show partial content relationships, not course equivalence.

concepts.text: A broad closest feasible response combining micro- and macroeconomics with accounting, finance, strategy, organisations, marketing, statistics, data, AI and research methods.

Economic theory and empirical methods examine public spending, distribution, incentives and economic change. Political and legal institutions, civil society and sustainability governance provide concrete ways to investigate how economic choices become public decisions.

Economics and financial-market, banking and monetary analysis are combined with econometrics, probability, calculus, programming, databases, machine learning and computational decisions under uncertainty. Quantitative methods support financial and economic inquiry; the programme does not reproduce Tilburg’s complete specialist business-economics sequence.

notes.text: Tilburg requires a combined economics-and-business curriculum, a 24-EC specialisation and a 12-EC thesis. The displayed external route is Bedrijfseconomie. The UCR options differ in business, data and public-policy emphasis and do not reproduce specialised management accounting, business administration, company law or sustainable finance. Optional independent research is additional to the displayed 180 EC.

descriptions.description: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
